comments.text:
Nice - this image makes the “what does the chart actually say?” question answerable, because the fine print matters a lot.

What this chart literally is (per the notes on the image)
---------------------------------------------------------

   Title: Chart 1 - AI scenarios
   Y-axis: GDP per capita in 1990 dollars (thousands), log scale (so 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 are doublings)
   Blue: Real GDP per capita (historical)
   Orange: Trend line fitted to 1870-2024, with 1.9% growth per year
   Green / Red / Purple: hypothetical paths based on different AI scenarios (their word: hypothetical)

That last line is the key: this is not “the Fed predicts extinction.” It is “here are example trajectories you could plug into an analysis.”

How to read it correctly
------------------------

Because it’s log scale, a straight line means “steady percentage growth.”

   The orange line is basically “the last 150 years keep going at 1.9%/year.”
   The blue line wiggles around it (wars, depression, postwar boom, etc.) but the long-run slope is similar.

So the chart is really showing: the long-run baseline has been remarkably stable, and then it draws three stylized AI disruptions.

What each scenario implies (and how extreme it really is)
---------------------------------------------------------

 1) Green - “AI GDP-boosted trend, 2.1% for 10 years”

This is deliberately modest.

   It’s only +0.2 percentage points for a decade.
   That compounds to roughly 2% higher GDP per capita level than the baseline by 2050 (not 20%, not 200%). In other words: meaningful, but not world-ending or world-transforming.

 2) Red - “Singularity: Benign scenario”

On a log chart, the red line curves upward sharply - which means it’s not just “faster growth,” it’s accelerating growth (super-exponential).

   Visually it jumps from roughly the low-$30k range (1990 dollars) to well above $100k (1990 dollars) within a relatively short window.
   That’s “runaway productivity” territory, not normal economics.

 3) Purple - “Singularity: Extinction”

GDP per capita collapses to near zero.

   This is basically a definitional move: if society collapses or humans are gone, measured GDP goes to 0.
   It’s a stress-test curve, not a measured projection.

What the existence of the chart does (and does not) prove
---------------------------------------------------------

 It does prove

   The authors thought it was reasonable to include fat-tail outcomes (huge upside, huge downside) in a public-facing scenario figure.
   It’s a sign that “AI could be macroeconomically discontinuous” is now discussable in mainstream institutions.

 It does not prove

   That extinction is likely.
   That a singularity will happen by a specific year.
   That the Fed is forecasting these outcomes.
   That GDP is the right yardstick if AI radically changes how value is created (GDP can become a bad proxy in extreme futures).

The most important “gotcha” in how people use this chart online
---------------------------------------------------------------

People often treat it like: “Look, the Fed says we hit a fork before 2035.”  
But the chart itself is closer to: “If you want to model AI as anything from a small productivity bump to a discontinuity, here are example paths.”

Notice what’s missing:

   No probabilities.
   No mechanism description on the figure (what causes red or purple).
   No constraints (energy, materials, geopolitics, regulation).
   No distributional story (GDP per capita can rise while many people get poorer).

A grounded takeaway
-------------------

If you strip the drama away, the chart is basically saying:

   For 150+ years, per-capita output has followed a steady exponential trend.
   A small AI productivity boost looks like a small upward shift (green).
   If you believe in true discontinuities (runaway or collapse), the curves become qualitatively different (red/purple).
   The policy-relevant point is less “pick red or purple” and more “we should not assume the future is just orange.”

You’re calling it “AGI” because that’s the label the authors use, not because anyone can define it in a precise or testable way. “AGI” remains a vague term, and that vagueness is doing a lot of rhetorical work.

The graph you’re showing assumes progress moves in one continuous direction—up and to the right. That’s a naïve assumption. Complex systems don’t evolve linearly; they jump, stall, regress, and break. Presenting smooth curves isn’t analysis, it’s marketing.

Handing systems with emergent, poorly understood behavior the ability to affect people’s livelihoods is inherently risky. Once deployed at scale, unpredictability isn’t a bug—it’s a structural hazard.

Learning systems don’t need intentions to create self-reinforcing dynamics. Optimization, persistence, and expansion can emerge without anything resembling human motives.

And it’s unrealistic to believe moral ideals will slow this down. The incentives are too strong: competition, capital, prestige, and national interest. People don’t build these systems because it’s safe or wise—they build them because they can, and because someone else will if they don’t
